Response to REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This study investigates the in vivo phase separation behavior of a membrane protein, LacY, in Escherichia
coli by artificially inducing condensate formation through fusion with the PopTag domain. The authors
further examine how membrane curvature, osmotic stress, and co-expression with LacZ influence the
localization and functionality of these condensates.
I have several concerns and comments:
(1) There remains unclear to what extent this artificially induced phase separation can be extrapolated to
naturally occurring phenomena.
The PopTag-LacY fusion is artificial, but it will serve as a valuable tool for elucidating the liquid-liquid phase
separation (LLPS) behavior of native transmembrane proteins. We empahsize that many membrane
proteins have intrinsically disordered cytoplasmic regions (IDRs), forming accessory domains of poorly
understood functions (10.1016/j.bbamem.2015.08.002, 10.1371/journal.pone.0158594,
10.1007/s00018-017-2562-5, 10.1021/cb200231c). These IDRs can potentially drive LLPS in native
membrane proteins. We use PopTag as a well characterized condensation-inducing tag to mimic this
process and investigate its structural and functional implications for the well-studied lactose permease
LacY. We added text in the introduction (lines 60 – 63 and 83 - 90) to make the rationale and benefit of
the system clearer.
(2) The fluorescence recovery of LacYmEos-Pop is reported to be only ~20%, which is notably low for a
bona fide phase-separated system. Such limited recovery raises concerns about whether the observed
structures truly represent dynamic condensates. Moreover, the possibility that the observed recovery
arises, at least in part, from the reactivation of fluorescent proteins from a dark state rather than from
molecular exchange cannot be excluded. The authors should address this point and consider additional
controls or experiments to distinguish between these possibilities.
This is an important point. We extended the FRAP dataset and carefully reanalyzed the data (see lines 561
- 569). Additional data and a different normalization procedure resulted in ~10% recovery fraction for
LacY-mEos-Pop, which is similar to what has been reported for the original cytoplasmic PopTag
[10.1038/s41467-024-47330-4] and other self-condensing proteins, e.g. aggresomes
[10.1126/sciadv.abh2929]. In 10.1038/s41467-024-47330-4, the authors attribute the partial recovery to
“gel-like” state of condensates. In our case, complete recovery is not possible because a substantial
fraction (>30%) of total fluorescence is irreversibly lost during bleaching of a pole. Further, the equilibrium
shortly after bleaching is partial because protein exchange between poles and lateral membrane is much
faster than protein transfer from one pole to another. We now also measured FRAP at the lateral
membrane and observed no recovery, also pointing towards the trapping of the LacYPop to the polar
condensates. Lateral membrane bleaching has been added to Figure 1d (lines 135 - 141). Importantly, the
diffusion of LacYPop molecules within the pole condensates is only 4% lower (within the error margin) than
in lateral condensates, and thus the system is dynamic with a very high partitioning of the condensate-
forming molecules.
We performed a series of additional experiments to address the concerns of the reviewer: (i) Bleaching
experiments on entire cells resulted in no recovery of fluorescence, indicating that the observed recovery
at polar condensates is not due to reactivation of the fluorescent protein. (ii) Fluorescence recovery at
the poles of chloramphenicol-treated cells was similar to that of untreated cells, demonstrating that
recovery is not caused by synthesis of new protein. Data is presented on Figure 1d and details of these
control experiments are provided in lines 137 – 141 and 574 – 579.
(3) In line 100, the authors states that the apparent size of the clusters is smaller, presumably due to
reduction of the “motion blur”. However, I am skeptical that motion blur alone could account for such a
substantial change in cluster size. Motion blur typically affects localization precision and overall resolution
in PALM imaging. In this context, it is unclear whether the observed spot size truly reflects the physical
size of the clusters or merely the resolution limit of the imaging system. Clarification and quantification is
needed.
By “motion blur” we mean that in our PALM reconstructions the localization of proteins was averaged
over either 6 min (~20 000 frames) or 30 min (~100 000 frames). In live cells, where protein condensates
can move in the membrane, this leads to a “motion blur”, which is less pronounced at shorter
reconstruction times. In fixed cells, where protein condensates do not move, the “motion blur” is less but
individual molecules still diffuse, which affects the localization precision. We find that localization
precision calculated for living and fixed E. coli BW25113 LacYmEos3-Pop are similar: 25±13 nm for living and
24±13 nm for fixed cells. To clarify concerns of the reviewer, we changed the text (lines 121 - 124).
(4) Moreover, the actual cluster dimensions are difficult to assess, as the scale bar is missing from Figure
1b. Please include it. The authors should also consider potential fixation-induced alterations in the
appearance of phase-separated structures (Irgen-Gioro, Yoshida et al. eLife 2022;11:e79903).
Scale bars have been added to figure 1b. Although we cannot fully exclude fixation-induced artifacts,
our fixed and living cells look very similar in a widefield microscope (see images below), unlike images in the
paper given by the reviewer.
(5) Additional methodological details are needed: what was the exposure time used for PALM imaging?
Furthermore, a color bar indicating localization counts should be added to Figure 1b to facilitate
comparison between live and fixed cells.
We introduced color bars in Figure 1b. For PALM image reconstructions we used 2D Gaussian rendering,
which takes into account localization uncertainties of individual molecules. Therefore, intensity in the
reconstructed images are roughly proportional to localization counts, but measured in a.u. instead of
counts/pixel. We provide these and other technical details on PALM imaging in the Methods section (lines
617 – 625).
(6) The co-condensation of LacY and LacZ is intriguing; however, the functional assay reveals a decrease
in β-galactosidase activity in heterocondensates compared to LacZPop alone. The underlying cause of this
reduction remains unclear. The authors should clarify whether it results from molecular crowding within
the condensate, altered conformational dynamics, or imbalances in protein expression levels.
Additionally, quantitative co-localization analysis between LacYPop and LacZPop would strengthen the
microscopy-based conclusions and provide a clearer picture of heterocondensate architecture.
We added a discussion on the reduced LacZ β-galactosidase activity in heterocondensates in lines 455 -
463. We have no evidence that the reduced activity is due to a lower expression level or different
crowding. We propose that the activity is related to the shape and size of the condensates, thus the
membrane-assisted 2D or 2.5D condensates are less active presumably due to a different stabilization of
LacZ oligomers than in the 3D homocondensates.
To quantify the co-localization between LacYPop and LacZPop, we calculated Pearson correlation coefficients
with Costes thresholding for all conditions, presented on the Fig. 5a, see new test in lines 315 - 319.
(7) Key quantitative parameters—such as the intracellular density of LacY-Pop, absolute copy numbers,
and the stoichiometry between PopTag and LacY—are not reported, limiting the ability to assess the
physiological relevance of the observed effects.
Thank you for pointing this out. We now performed in-gel fluorescence analysis of of LacYmEos and LacYmEos-
Pop fusion proteins using cell lysates (see new Fig. S6), and we determined absolute protein concentrations
using calibration with known amounts of a purified mEos3.2 fused to thioredoxin-1 (TrxAmEos). Absolute
copy numbers of LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop are 3.5 ± 0.4 x 103 and 3.4 ± 0.5 x 103 proteins/cell respectively,
which are similar to the copy number of native LacY (~2.5 x 103 proteins per cell, doi:
10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002010). Thus, expressed LacY protein amounts to less than 1% of total membrane
protein. These new results are presented in lines 267 - 272 and Supplemental figure S6.
If the question of the reviewer regarding stoichiometry relates to the ratio between the PopTags to LacY
molecules within the cells, the ratio is 1:1, as they are expressed as a fusion protein. If, instead, the
question refers to the number of interactions between different LacYPop molecules, this is estimated to
range between one and three, since the α-helices of PopTag are expected to act as the interaction motifs
(“stickers”) driving condensate formation. However, the precise number of such interactions cannot be
determined.
(8) The Supplementary Videos are missing.
Supplementary videos have been added.
(9) The title is too broad and should specify the particular membrane protein being studied.
We changed the title to “Structural and functional implications of in vivo phase separation of membrane
protein LacY in Escherichia coli”
(10) LacY lacks intrinsic disordered regions (IDRs) and does not phase-separate in its native state. PopTag
is an orthogonally introduced multivalent module that does not interfere with endogenous phase-
separation systems. This important background information is not sufficiently explained in the
Introduction and should be clearly stated to justify the system design.
We modified the introduction to emphasize these points (lines 83 - 90).
(11) There are inconsistencies between Figure 1e and Figure 1f. The figure legend appears to reverse the
image order: “Diffusion maps of E. coli BW25113 LacYmEos (top) and BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop (bottom)”
may be incorrectly labeled.
Thanks for noticing, the legend has been changed and is now in line with the Figures 1e and 1f; figures 1f
and 1g in the revised manuscript.
(12) In Supplementary Table 2, some primer sequences include the base “U”. If this represents modified
nucleotides (e.g., RNA bases), please clarify; otherwise, verify and correct the sequences.
Uracil nucleotides are included in all the primers used for USER cloning. Uracils are needed to enable
recognition and cleavage by the USER (Uracil-Specific Excision Reagent) Enzyme to create sticky ends. This
point is now explained in the legend of Supplementary Table 2.
(13) The manuscript contains several formatting issues that should be addressed. For instance, extraneous
lines are present in Figure 2; line 254 refers to “3d” but should cite “Figure 3d”; the font size in Figure 4 is
inconsistent with other figures; and the Supplementary information includes two entries labeled “Figure
S8” on pages 11 and 14, respectively.
We apologize for these mistakes, and they have now been corrected.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors probe the impact of condensation at cellular membrane on the activity of the protein LacY in
E. Coli. LacY is a transmembrane protein. To achieve this, they fuse a pop tag (the c-terminal domain of
popZ) to LacY and probe the condensation of the protein. using a combination of experimental and
computational methods. They also probe the effect of co-condensation (ie of a membrane, LacY, and
cytosolic protein, LacZ) on protein activity. For this they make fusions of LacY and LacZ, with and without
pop tags and express them together in various combinations. The main highlights of the paper are:
I. The LacY-pop fusion forms condensates with different propensities at the poles vs lateral regions of the
membrane
II. They provide evidence suggesting that this is due to differences in membrane curvature in these two
regions
III. They also show that the LacY-pop fusion leads to slightly higher substrate transport, compared to the
LacY without the pop tag
IV. The LacY-pop fusion also leads to better lactose uptake under osmotic stress conditions
V. They observe co-condensation of LacY and LacZ, but this co-condensation does not lead to increased
activity; it even seems to suppress the activity.
In general, the manuscript is well written, and it is an interesting study. However, some of the conclusions
are not fully supported by the data presented and certain methodological details are missing, as outlined
below:
Major remarks:
1. The authors measure the protein diffusion at the poles and in the lateral regions for LacY-pop and find
that they are similar. They should also perform FRAP separately for the poles and the lateral condensates.
This will add further confidence that the material properties are similar.
We find that the diffusion inside the condensates is the same at the poles and in the lateral membrane,
which is based on the single-molecule measurements (Figure 1f,g). Bleaching of individual condensates at
the lateral membrane is not possible, due to their small size. However, FRAP of the lateral membrane
showed no recovery (new Figure 1d and text in lines 135 - 141), which might be due to the very strong
partitioning of LacYPop in the polar condensates.
2. For the MD simulation the initial set up is not ideal for an unbiased comparison. They start with the
proteins evenly spaced, using the same spacing for the LacY and LacY-pop. However, the Lac-Y pop will on
average have a larger radius of gyration, which means that the probability that the proteins can find each
other and interact will naturally be greater. The authors should use a non-biased initial set up where the
spacing scales with the average protein size. Additionally, another robust test would be start from a case
where the proteins are already clustered and measure whether the clustering at equilibrium are
significantly different.
We thank the reviewer for this comment on a potential bias in our initial simulation setup. We have
extended our simulations to 50 μs, which is sufficiently long to observe multiple binding and unbinding
events of the membrane proteins, ensuring the initial configuration does not bias our analysis of cluster
stability and size. The new data presented in Figure 2
3. The criteria used for determining if a cluster is formed in the MD simulation seems quite weak. They
put two proteins in cluster if at least they share one residue-residue contact. What is the average strength
of such a contact in comparison to the average thermal energy (KT)? Ideally, such interactions should be
multiples of KT to constitute a viable contact.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Our clustering criterion was designed to capture
large-scale differences in clustering behavior between LacY and LacYPop in an interpretable manner. This
approach revealed the clustering differences, which were validated with extended 50 μs simulations
during revision.
The energetic basis for these clustering differences is significant. Our contact map analysis (Figure 2c)
shows that PopTag-PopTag interactions occur primarily through the amphipathic α-helices, mainly the
hydrophobic interfaces of helix 1 and 2. Each helix contains approximately 15 residues. Literature values
for hydrophobic interactions range from 0.5-2 kT per residue
(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2011.02.053), meaning a single helical interface has a significant favorable
energy. Additionally, the proteins in larger clusters engage through multiple PopTag-PopTag contacts
simultaneously.
4. Related to that are the number of protein-protein interactions normalized by protein size? For instance,
the mutant with the pop tag will naturally have more contacts because it has more residues. Please discuss
in greater detail whether the reported protein-protein contacts are normalized or not.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this clarification. The reported protein-protein contacts are not
normalized by protein size as they are counted per membrane protein, not per residue. Our primary focus
was on the qualitative clustering behavior, whether proteins form contacts or not, rather than quantifying
absolute residue contact numbers. We have clarified this point in the revised text (legend to the Figure
2d).
5. Based on figure 2 and the SI, the authors claim that pop-tag interactions are primarily driven by helix 1.
The data presented only partially supports this. Based on fig 2c, a large fraction of the contacts are
localized in the region between H1 and H2. They do not comment on this. They also report that the
interactions are primarily hydrophobic in nature. However, the intermediate regions, seem to be charged
regions. Are they? Or at least regions with low hydrophobicity. If so, it seems that charged or other
interactions are a key.
We thank the reviewer for this observation. The extended simulations performed during revision now
reveal much more pronounced helix 2 involvement in LacYPop, with clear helix 1-helix 2 and helix 2-helix 2
interactions. The H1-H2 linker also shows contacts due to its hydrophobic residues, alongside charged
residues (ASP36, LYS35, ARG38). Additionally, when helices 1 and 2 from different PopTag domains
interact antiparallel, their connecting linker regions are brought into proximity, increasing the contacts.
We conclude that hydrophobic interactions are the primary driving force for PopTag condensation. We
have clarified this in the revised text to acknowledge the contributions of the H1-H2 linker region to the
contact map. See changes in lines 184 – 185 and 190 – 192.
6. In Fig 2b, it is unclear why the slab geometry was used to determine the contacts for the pop-tag
condensate in figure 2c. Ideally, this measurement is done on an isotropic system to avoid the effects of
having interfaces.
We used a slab geometry as a standard protocol for building condensates without knowing the
equilibrium density beforehand, while maximizing the internal condensate region and minimizing
interface effects. To validate this approach, we calculated the condensate density from the slab
simulations and constructed an isotropic condensate simulation at this density. This simulation was run
for 20 μs and used to calculate a reference contact map. Comparison of the contact maps shows that
interaction patterns qualitatively agree between both geometries, confirming that our slab-derived
contact analysis accurately represents the inter-PopTag interactions.
7. In the experiments, it would be useful to characterize the material properties of the heterogeneous
condensates, as done for the single-protein ones. This may help shed light on why the activity is affected
in the manner reported.
We now performed FRAP measurements in cells with LacYPop with co-expression of LacZPop. We observed
the same recovery pattern as for cell expressing LacYPop alone, that is, similar half-times of recovery (122
± 36 seconds for LacYmEos-Pop alone vs. 103 ± 19 seconds for LacYmEos-Pop in heterocondensate, extra sum-of-
squares F test p-value = 0.7620) and extents of recovery (0.132 ± 0.007 for LacYmEos-Pop alone vs. 0.128 ±
0.009 for LacYmEos-Pop in heterocondensate, extra sum-of-squares F test p-value = 0.6958) (lines 320 - 327
and Supplementary Figure S7). Information about the statistical test is added to the “Statistical analysis”
section lines 746-748 Thus, on the basis of FRAP experiments, we find no difference in the material
properties of LacYPop in homo- and heterocondensate.
8. The structures from alphafold3 used for setting up the simulations were these relaxed via all-atom
simulations before using martinize2? Are the secondary structures static in the martini simulations or are
they allowed to fluctuate?
The AlphaFold3 structures were used directly without prior all-atom relaxation. We validated these
structures by comparing them to available crystal structures of LacY, which showed good agreement with
the experimental models.
In our Martini simulations, secondary structures are constrained using an elastic network model,
preventing changes in secondary structure elements. However, the proteins are still allowed to fluctuate
and move within these constraints, maintaining realistic dynamics at the coarse-grained level. While
allowing changes in secondary structure could provide additional model accuracy, we deemed this beyond
the scope of the current study since our primary focus was on protein-protein interactions mediated by
PopTag domains. See changes in lines 652 – 659.
9. What is the rationale for the pressure set up used in the slab simulations? What are these so-called
default pressure parameters?
The slab simulation pressure setup makes the system incompressible in the xy-directions, keeping the
interface area fixed, while allowing the z-axis (box height) to equilibrate and establish the correct
condensate density. This prevents artificial expansion or contraction of the slab interface while enabling
the condensate to find its natural thickness. The "default pressure parameters" refer to standard Martini3
pressure coupling settings (1 bar, τ_p = 12 ps, β = 3×10⁻⁴ bar⁻¹) applied in the xy-plane, while pressure
coupling in the z-direction is disabled to preserve the slab geometry. This information is now added in
lines 686 - 689.
10. The authors state that the Martini-parameters were tuned using the idr-tune flag. Please discuss in
greater detail what this means. Tuned in what sense?
The idr-tune flag is an option in Martinize2 that optimizes Martini force field parameters specifically for
intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Standard Martini parameters tend to over compact IDRs compared
to experimental observations. The idr-tune flag addresses this by adjusting the bonded interactions in the
Martini3 protein model to better reproduce the expanded conformations of disordered regions. This
parameter optimization has been validated to improve the correspondence with all-atom simulations and
experimental data (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58199-2). This information is now added in lines
666-667.
Minor remarks:
1. The caption of Figure 2 needs further details so readers can immediately tell what they are looking at.
For instance, mentioning that proteins are embedded in a membrane etc.
We thank the reviewer for indicating that this was not clear, we improved the figure legend to clarify.
2. Describe what are spheroplasts at first usage.
Description of spheroplasts has been added in lines 235-236
3. Labels are needed throughout Figure 1. It is difficult to tell what exactly one should be looking for in Fig
1G for instance.
We added arrows pointing to the edges of the membrane-anchored LacYmEos-Pop condensates in right panel
of Figure 1h, and we refer to them in the legend.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Key results
In this study the authors examine phase separation of membrane proteins in live E. coli cells by expressing
fusions composed of membrane protein LacY and a PopTag scaffold domain to drive phase separation.
They examine the effect of this tag on the localization, dynamics, and activity of LacY, and explore the
activity of downstream enzyme LacZ with or without the same tag. The manuscript is clearly written and
the topic is of interest, particularly on how engineered co-condensation at a membrane might affect
enzyme activity in a cascade. However, the authors’ mechanistic arguments should be strengthened with
additional evidence, and additional quantification/clarification is needed. The following are some points
for revision.
Major points
1. The introduction should include a review of the existing literature on membrane-localized biomolecular
condensates (surface wetting, biological significance, curvature remodeling, etc.). I would disagree with
the characterization that membrane protein phase separation is uncharted territory given the examples
mentioned in the introduction. I also wonder whether a dynamic protein monolayer counts as a
condensate if it does not recruit components from the bulk, as the classification can become unclear at
the nanoscale (though this broad question does not need to be addressed in this manuscript).
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We expanded the introduction with membrane-localized
condensates (lines 67 - 77). “Uncharted territory” is perhaps too strong, but the amount of mechanistic
insight in membrane-localized condensates is minimal. Text has been changed in lines 52 - 53. We now
refer to the membrane condensates as 2D condensates, but we notice that (based on our analysis) they
display all the features of classical 3D condensates except that components are recruited from the
membrane and not from the cytoplasm.
2. In Figure 1G, arrows or other indicators would be helpful as the thin layer is hard to see. What methods
were used to classify whether the layer was present in each image and measure its thickness?
We added arrows to Figure 1h (previously Figure 1g) indicating the edges of the electron-dense regions
on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane.
To classify the EM images, we inspected them visually and, first, selected those with intact membrane
integrity and periplasmic space. Then, the layer was identified as a distinct electron-dense region on the
cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane. The analysis was blinded to the experiment group and
independently performed by two researchers, only cells labeled as condensate positive by both
researchers were marked as “positive” in the final analysis.
To estimate the thickness of the layer, we analyzed line profiles of the electron density perpendicular to
the membrane using ImageJ. All this information is now added in the Methods section (lines 642 – 647).
3. The MD simulations do not include mEos3.2, but this domain contributes significant size and surface
charge to the whole protein construct, and these features can affect phase separation/protein-protein
interactions. Can the authors discuss how the MD results might change if they included this domain?
We thank the reviewer for this comment. mEos3.2 serves purely as a fluorescent reporter and is not
expected to influence the PopTag-mediated clustering mechanism we are investigating. mEos3.2 was
designed as a true monomeric protein (10.1038/nmeth.2021). Omitting mEos3.2 from our simulations
reduced the computational complexity.
4. Residue-membrane interactions competing with scaffold protein condensate formation is an
interesting idea. Since the alternate simulation setup in Fig S4 resulted in quite different interaction
networks from those in Fig 2, can the authors comment on which interactions might correspond better to
the observations in vivo?
We suggest a two-step process for the condensate formation of LacYPop: Initially, PopTags interact with
the membrane while exploring protein-protein contacts (Fig 2). As the local concentration increases,
protein-protein interactions dominate over membrane association, leading to PopTags interacting in
solution (Fig S4). Sampling these different states in separate simulations is necessary due to MD timescale
limitations. The full process of LacY-bound PopTags detaching from the membrane and forming
condensates in solution is beyond current simulation timescales. In cells, we expect PopTags initially
sample both membrane and protein interactions, with condensate formation occurring when protein-
protein interactions outcompete membrane association. These points are better articulated in the revised
manuscript (lines 203 - 206).
5. The experiments in Fig. 3 are interesting, especially the spheroplast-plasmolysis rescue experiment.
However, these figures are not enough evidence to make a claim that membrane curvature drives
condensate formation. Quantifying fluorescence intensity against local membrane curvature in the
datasets from Fig. 3d,e could support the claim that only the high-curvature regions promote condensate
formation (and provide an opportunity for larger sample size and a statistical test). Also, during osmotic
upshift there can be many changes to the intracellular chemical environment (ionic strength, pH,
crowding, etc.) which are known to govern biomolecular condensate phase separation. Are there ways to
confirm that the observed condensate formation is not due to one of these factors?
We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. We analyzed the correlation between local membrane
curvature and fluorescence intensity in LacYmEos-Pop spheroplasts, using the Kappa plugin for ImageJ
[https://github.com/fiji/Kappa]. This analysis confirmed modest but significant correlation (ρ=0.24,
p<0.0001; Spearman correlation). We added the plots for normalized fluorescence intensity and
normalized curvature as a Supplementary Figure S5, and we present the data in lines 256 - 258.
We agree that effects of ionic strength, pH, crowding and other parameters are affected by osmotic
upshift, and we cannot rule out that they play a role in the formation of 2D membrane condensates.
We also do not see ways to dissect these parameters in in vivo studies. Importantly, we do find the formation
of the condensates at the cell poles in non-stressed cells, that is, at “normal” ionic strength, pH and
crowding levels. We feel that local curvature effects are the most plausible explanation. We now discuss
these points in more detail (lines 428 - 433).
6. In Figure 4E deformed cells seem hard to detect in the PopTag fluorescence images, given that there is
mostly only signal near the poles. Can the authors show images where the morphology is easier to see?
We did not observe cell deformations with a 2-fold increase in osmolarity, using the LacYmEos-Pop expressing
strain. We changed the text in lines 283 - 288 to clarify this. For the 4-fold increase in osmolarity, the
zoom-in of the deformations is shown in Figure 4e.
Minor points
1. Several scale bar sizes are missing throughout the figure captions.
Scale bar sizes have been added to all the figure legends.
2. In Figure 1C, which dataset was quantified? It seems like datasets from different imaging methods (Fig.
1A-B) might give very different localization results.
The percentages in Figure 1c were calculated from single-protein localization microscopy. This
information has been added to the legend of Figure 1.
3. The authors say that condensation is primarily driven by Helix 1, but the contact map in Fig. 2C seems
to indicate that the linker between H1 and H2 plays an equally significant role. Could the authors
comment?
We thank the reviewer for this question. Our contact map analysis indeed shows significant H1-H2 linker
interactions.
Comparing our two systems shows that linker interactions appear more prominent in the membrane-
bound LacYPop simulation due to constrained geometry that brings linker regions into close proximity,
while the solution-mediated condensate simulation shows fewer linker contacts with mainly hydrophobic
residues of the linker interacting. This demonstrates that the high linker contacts arise from geometric
constraints (antiparallel interactions of PopTags) rather than residue-specific interactions.
We have clarified this in the revised text to acknowledge the contributions of the H1-H2 linker region to
the contact map.
4. The authors mention that “PopTags mediate interactions between otherwise non-associating LacY
proteins”, but simulated LacY proteins did cluster (Fig S3).
We thank the reviewer for this comment. During extended simulations performed for revision, we
observed more LacY clustering than expected, which lead us to revisit our simulation setup. We identified
that the inward-facing conformation predicted by AlphaFold3 (the most abundant state in the PDB)
induced local membrane curvature that promoted non-specific protein association. Since opening of the
periplasmic cavity is the rate-limiting step in LacY transport, the outward-facing conformation represents
the more prevalent protein conformation (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1112157108). We therefore
repeated all simulations with structural restraints derived from the outward-facing structure (PDB: 6VBG)
applied to the AlphaFold3 models (see revised methods).
With the corrected outward-facing conformation, LacY proteins exhibit substantially reduced clustering.
While some transient, dynamic clustering is observed, this is expected at the high protein densities used
in our simulations and does not lead to formation of large stable aggregates. In contrast, LacYPop forms
still form large clusters in our updated model, demonstrating that PopTag-mediated interactions drive the
observed membrane reorganization. All results in the manuscript have been updated using these
improved simulations.
5. In Figure S6 can the authors quantify protein level by gel densitometry, to support the argument that
the different construct activities in Fig 4 are not due to different expression levels?
We redid the experiments with in-gel fluorescence of LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop fusion proteins and using
calibration curves to quantify the levels of LacY. See also our response to comment 7 of reviewer 1. The
new data are presented in lines 267 - 272 and new Supplemental figure S6.
6. Significance signs are missing in Figure S8.
We added the significance signs to the supplementary Figure S9 (previously Figure S8).
7. In Figure S10 the monomer band does not appear to be ~145 kDa, based on the ladder.
mRuby fluorescent protein remains folded in SDS-PAA gels, as we observe its fluorescence signal. Hence,
the electrophoretic mobility of LacZ-mRuby fusions is higher than predicted from their molecular weight.
We clarify this point in the legend of Figure S11 (previously Figure S10).
8. A typo: “Having characterized the structure and interactions of LacZPop membrane condensates
experimentally and computationally” I think the authors meant to write LacYPop.
We thank the reviewer for catching this typo. We have corrected "LacZPop" to "LacYPop".

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I believe that most of my earlier questions have been addressed and I appreciate the authors’ clarifications. I will leave it to the editor to evaluate the significance of this work. Moreover, I still have several concerns:
In the FRAP experiments, different bleaching conditions were used (different microscopes, objectives, bleaching schemes (1× vs 30× at 100%), different readout intensities and time resolutions). Could the authors clarify why these parameters differed?
Additionally, the comparison between fluorescence recovery at the polar and lateral membranes is an important aspect of the authors’ interpretation. However, the Methods section does not describe whether the same ROI size, bleaching area, and laser power were used for both regions. This is important for the repeatbility of this work.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: Thanks to the authors for thoroughly addressing most of the points raised in the initial review. However, the contact analysis for determining the protein clusters remains weak. The authors should assess the dependence of the cluster/contact analysis on their criterion. One shared residue is a very soft criterion for determining clusters. Also, this should be compared to KT in the simulation. Additionally the residues have different sizes, so a global cutoff of 15A for determining contacts is rather crude. Instead this cutoff should be residue-size dependent.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors have improved the manuscript with additional quantification, improved simulations, and expanded text and methodological details. The manuscript is suitable for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
I believe that most of my earlier questions have been addressed and I appreciate
the authors’ clarifications. I will leave it to the editor to evaluate the significance of
this work. Moreover, I still have several concerns:
In the FRAP experiments, different bleaching conditions were used (different
microscopes, objectives, bleaching schemes (1× vs 30× at 100%), different
readout intensities and time resolutions). Could the authors clarify why these
parameters differed?
Additionally, the comparison between fluorescence recovery at the polar and
lateral membranes is an important aspect of the authors’ interpretation. However,
the Methods section does not describe whether the same ROI size, bleaching area,
and laser power were used for both regions. This is important for the repeatbility of
this work.
We used two different microscopes because the Zeiss LSM 710 microscope was
broken after the measurements with LacYmEos were completed. After that, we
measured FRAP with LacYmEos-Pop on a newly purchased Leica Stellaris 8. The
readout intensities were adjusted to achieve similar image quality with the two
different setups.
Our experiments show that condensated LacYmEos-Pop and non-condensated
LacYmEos have very different localization and mechanical properties and thus
require different parameters for optimal FRAP recordings. Therefore, we adjusted
the number of bleaching steps and the time-steps in the recovery measurements
depending on the sample. For LacYmEos, the fluorescence recovery occurred within
seconds, and therefore, shorter bleaching was necessary to avoid the loss of signal
in the entire cell, and shorter time-steps were used to follow the recovery. In
contrast, for LacYmEos-Pop, the content exchange between polar condensates was
slow; near-complete bleaching of one cell pole required 30 bleaching steps but did
not lead to much loss of fluorescence at the opposite cell pole, and the recovery
happened only on the timescale of minutes (see Supplementary Figure S1).
Because of these dramatic differences in protein behaviour, recovery could not be
reasonably measured at the same settings for LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop.
We had used either 3% or 10% of readout laser power for the bleaching of polar

Because of the new measurements, our estimates of the extent of recovery and

Thanks to the authors for thoroughly addressing most of the points raised in the
initial review. However, the contact analysis for determining the protein clusters
remains weak. The authors should assess the dependence of the cluster/contact
analysis on their criterion. One shared residue is a very soft criterion for
determining clusters. Also, this should be compared to KT in the simulation.
Additionally the residues have different sizes, so a global cutoff of 15A for
determining contacts is rather crude. Instead this cutoff should be residue-size
dependent.
We thank the reviewer for this constructive feedback on improving the robustness
of our contact analysis. To address the concern about using a global cutoff, we
validated our approach by comparing contact detection using all beads per residue
(cutoff 1.5 nm) versus only backbone beads (cutoff 1.0 nm). While the different
2
cutoffs detect slightly different absolute numbers of contacts, the clustering
behaviour and trends remain consistent between both methods (SFig. S5, panel

To assess whether contacts represent meaningful interactions beyond thermal

pairs in clusters interact through multiple residues. Applying stricter contact
thresholds slightly varies individual cluster sizes but preserves all the key trends in
our analysis, confirming that our conclusions are robust to the choice of contact
criterion.
These validation analyses confirm that our contact criterion reliably captures the

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) controls protein activity and dynamically organizes (macro)molecules in living systems without the need for membrane-bound compartments. Biomolecular condensates of water-soluble proteins have extensively been studied, but little is known about LLPS of membrane proteins. In this work we induce in vivo condensation of lactose permease (LacY), a widely-studied model monomeric inner membrane protein in Escherichia coli, and evaluate how it affects LacY function. We fused LacY with engineered, condensate-forming protein PopTag. We observe major changes in the localization and mobility of LacYPop. Molecular dynamics simulations show how the PopTag domain drives the condensate-like association dynamics of LacYPop through hydrophobic sticker interactions. LacYPop preserves native-level transport activity and outperforms the non-condensed LacY under mild hyperosmotic stress (osmotic upshift). In osmotically stressed cells, membrane-bound biomolecular condensates also reduce deformation of the cytoplasmic membrane. Perturbation experiments suggest that membrane curvature drives the accumulation of LacYPop at the poles of E. coli. Co-condensation of LacY and β-galactosidase LacZ slightly reduces their activity and results in remarkable cellular reorganization of the proteins. Our research shows the localization, dynamics, and function of phase-separated membrane proteins in bacteria and highlights the potential of LLPS for engineering complex metabolic networks in vivo.

---

## Introduction

Phase separation of biomolecules is an emerging field of cell biology1,2. Numerous examples of liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) have been discovered in eukaryotic cells (e.g., nucleoli, Cajal bodies, stress granules, U-bodies, etc.3). The physico-chemical properties of condensates, such as viscosity, pH, oxygen concentration, and molecular composition, can differ from the surrounding milieu, favoring or disfavoring certain reactions and interactions4. The propensity of a molecule to partition in a condensate relative to the surrounding medium typically also differs. Formation of biomolecular condensates of protein and/or nucleic acids is governed by attractive intermolecular interactions between motifs in intrinsically disordered regions (IDR), the so-called stickers-and-spacers framework, or repeats of folded domains with connecting linkers5. The ability of a macromolecule to interact with multiple partners simultaneously (multivalency) is a requirement for phase separation6.

The fraction of water-soluble proteins with IDRs is 30–40% in mammalian cells, but is thought to be lower in bacteria3. A subfraction of these molecules enables multivalent interactions that drive biomolecular condensation. Little is known of the phase separation of transmembrane proteins driven by intermolecular protein interactions. Some examples are T-cell receptors in mammalian cells, Rv1747 protein in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and PodJ in Caulobacter vibrioides. The phase separation of T-cell receptors and their auxiliary proteins plays a role in the transduction of signals within the immune system7. The phase separation and 2D clustering of the ATP-binding cassette transporter Rv1747 is promoted by condensation of two Forkhead-associated cytosolic domains linked by an IDR and tuned by phosphorylation8. In PodJ protein part of the cytosolic coiled-coil domain and IDR are responsible for the condensate formation9. We note that IDRs are present in numerous types of membrane proteins and often implicated in their regulation, but they are generally not seen as a possibility for condensation of the proteins and putative multivalency effects have not been explored10–12. Next to protein-driven phase separation, membrane proteins can be organized via scaffolding proteins like flotillins13,14 or partition differentially in liquid-disordered and liquid-ordered lipid domains in the membrane15, but these mechanisms are not relevant for this study.

Biomolecular condensates of water-soluble proteins can physically associate with the lipid bilayer, but they are not inserted into the membrane16. Such condensates are generally composed of proteins, often with intrinsically disordered regions, and/or nucleic acids, enabling multivalent interactions that drive condensate formation. Membrane association can occur through electrostatic interactions, lipid-binding domains, or curvature-sensing motifs, leading to surface wetting, local membrane deformation, and curvature remodeling. This type of membrane-condensate interaction can remodel membrane morphology through capillary forces, induce nanoscale ruffling at the condensate–membrane interface, and couple protein phase separation to lipid phase behavior. Such condensates are attributed important biological roles, including spatial regulation of signaling pathways, organization of cytoskeletal elements, facilitation of endocytic events, and remodeling of organelle surfaces.

To study the mechanisms and implications of multivalent site-specific interactions between soluble regions of membrane proteins in vivo, we use the condensation domain PopTag to drive phase separation of an integral membrane protein. PopTag is the C-terminal part of the phase-separating protein PopZ, which is important for the asymmetrical division of Caulobacter vibrioides17,18. PopTag consists of three sticker sequences separated by IDRs, allowing multivalent interactions and thus condensate formation. We fused this protein tag to the C-terminus of lactose permease LacY of Escherichia coli. LacY natively lacks intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs); it does not undergo phase separation and is homogenously distributed in the inner membrane. E. coli lacks PopZ orthologues; therefore, introduction of PopTag should be orthogonal to native phase-separating systems. Our synthetic system of a polytopic membrane protein fused to a condensation-driving domain mimics features widely present in transmembrane proteins and can serve as a platform to investigate structural and functional implications of LLPS of membrane proteins10,19. Addition of PopTag to LacY results in a predominantly polar localization of the fusion protein. We show the condensate-like behavior of LacYPop fused to a fluorescent protein mEos3.2 (LacYmEos-Pop, Supplementary Table 1) by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), photoactivated localization microscopy (PALM), and single-molecule displacement mapping (SMdM). Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, we show how the PopTag domains bridge LacY proteins through hydrophobic sticker interactions and form a dynamic network of protein–protein associations leading to condensate formation. In a series of perturbation experiments, we show that nucleoid exclusion is not critical for the polar localization, while local membrane curvature plays a role. Using 14C-lactose transport experiments, we show that LacY is fully active in condensates and even outperforms native LacY. Finally, we designed and characterized heterocondensates of LacYPop with its downstream lactose-metabolizing enzyme, β-galactosidase (LacZ)-PopTag (LacZPop).

---

## Results

PopTag induces biomolecular condensation of LacY in the inner membrane of E. coli
Genes for LacY-mEos3.2 and LacY-mEos3.2-PopTag fusions were inserted into the pBAD vector and transformed into E. coli BW25113, resulting in BW25113 LacYmEos and BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop. Wide-field fluorescence microscopy shows that LacYmEos is equally distributed in the inner membrane, without preferred localization, whereas LacYmEos-Pop is predominantly present at the cell poles but discrete foci are also visible at the lateral membrane (Fig. 1a). To reveal fine details of LacYmEos-Pop clusters we performed PALM microscopy with live cells and cells fixed with formaldehyde–glutaraldehyde (4% w/v formaldehyde, 0.4% w/v glutaraldehyde in 100 mM sucrose dissolved in MQ water) (Fig. 1b). In live cells, single-molecule localizations, recorded for 30 min (~100.000 frames), show patterns akin those of the wide-field fluorescence microscopy images, whereas reconstructions recorded for 6 min (~20,000 frames) reveal multiple clusters on the lateral membrane, similar to what has been seen for Rv1747 in M. tuberculosis8. The fraction of localizations at the cell poles is two times higher for LacYmEos-Pop (0.62±0.06) than for LacYmEos (0.30±0.04) (Fig. 1c). In fixed cells, the localization of LacYmEos-Pop is preserved, but the apparent size of the clusters is smaller, presumably due to reduction of the “motion blur” (Supplementary Video 1). The difference in cluster size observed in PALM reconstructions reflects the physical size of the clusters and is not due to a different localization precision, which is similar for live (25±13 nm) and fixed (24±13 nm) BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop cells. Thus, LacYmEos-Pop predominantly localizes at cell poles and forms mobile foci in the lateral membrane that become immobile upon fixation.

To investigate the mobility of LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop, we performed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and single-molecule displacement mapping (SMdM20–22) experiments. The fluorescence recovery of LacYmEos-Pop had a half-time of 134±47 s and reached ~14% of the initial fluorescence, and the majority of the molecules partition inside punctuated condensates upon recovery (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 1). Non-condensed LacYmEos recovered with a half-time of 0.61±0.14 s and reached ~72% of the initial fluorescence (Fig. 1e). The moderate recovery of LacYmEos-Pop reflects protein exchange between the biomolecular condensate at the bleached pole and the lateral membrane (small fraction of total LacYmEos-Pop); the fluorescence of the non-bleached pole does not change during the recovery phase. Photobleaching of the lateral membrane did not result in fluorescence recovery, indicating that LacYPop is tightly sequestered within the polar condensates. The recovery at the poles is not due to reactivation of the fluorescent protein, because we saw no recovery of fluorescence when cells were fully photobleached (Fig. 1d). Furthermore, the fluorescence recovery at the poles is not caused by synthesis of new protein, because the recovery was similar in untreated and translation inhibitor (chloramphenicol)-treated cells.

Next, we examined the mobility of individual LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop molecules with SMdM23 (Fig. 1f). The apparent diffusion coefficient (D) of LacYmEos is lower at the cell poles compared to the lateral membrane (D=0.17±0.04 versus 0.22±0.06 μm2/s, two-sided t-test p-value=0.0002) (Fig. 1g). This decrease in D suggests a lower protein mobility at the cell poles but can also be a result of two-dimensional projection of protein movement across the membrane. The apparent diffusion coefficient of LacYmEos-Pop is similar between the cell poles and the lateral membrane (D=0.11±0.02 vs. 0.12±0.01 μm2/s, two-sided t-test p-value=0.34) and is 35% lower than that of polar LacYmEos. Since LacYmEos-Pop mobility in the lateral membrane and at the cell pole is reduced to a similar extent, we conclude that LacYmEos-Pop forms not only large condensates at the cell poles, but also smaller condensates in the lateral membrane.

We performed transmission electron microscopy on cryo-fixed BW25113 LacYmEos and BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop cells to verify the membrane localization of LacYmEos-Pop condensates at higher resolution than observed by light microscopy. We observe electron-dense regions on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane at the cell pole in 4 out of 6 BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop cells and in 2 out of 10 BW25113 LacYmEos cells (Fig. 1h, Supplementary Fig. 3). The approximate thickness of these regions is 10 nm, which is similar to the predicted length of the mEos3.2-PopTag part of LacYmEos-Pop. Remarkably, the shape and integrity of the inner membrane adjacent to the electron-dense regions at the cell poles are preserved. These data suggest that LacYmEos-Pop condensates anchor to the inner membrane without deforming it. Collectively, our observations suggest that LacYmEos-Pop form two-dimensional biomolecular condensates in the inner membrane of E. coli, with large condensates at the cell poles and smaller ones in the lateral membrane.

Hydrophobic stickers drive LacYPop condensation
To investigate how the fused PopTag influences the organization of LacY in the membrane, we performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of nine LacY proteins in an E. coli-like lipid membrane, with and without a PopTag (Fig. 2a). The simulations were executed in triplicate for better statistics on our observations. The proteins were initially positioned in equally spaced grid configurations. During a 50 μs simulation, both proteins show a clear difference in clustering behavior. LacY proteins without a PopTag formed relatively static small clusters, maintaining approximately three separate clusters throughout the simulation. In contrast, LacYPop proteins show substantially more dynamic interactions, ultimately forming one large cluster during the simulations. Quantitative analysis confirms this difference in clustering dynamics (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 4), with LacYPop having more fluctuations in the number of protein–protein interactions, indicating the dynamic nature of the formed contacts.

To understand the molecular mechanism behind the PopTag-mediated clustering, we analyzed the specific residue contacts involved in PopTag–PopTag interactions. First, we performed simulations of the PopTag alone (Fig. 2b). The contact map analysis reveals that inter-PopTag interactions in condensates are primarily driven by helix 1 (residues 14–31) and helix 2 (residues 40–58), with notable contacts also observed in the H1–H2 linker region (Fig. 2c, right panel). We then determined the contacts formed by PopTag when fused to LacY in the membrane and found again that H1 and H2 are the primary drivers of inter-PopTag interactions (Fig. 2c, left panel). The interaction interface in both cases is dominated by the amphipathic ɑ-helices with high hydrophobic moment. The hydrophobic faces of these putative helices most likely form the “stickers” for condensation, as indicated by the hydrophobicity profile along the residue index. Contacts in the H1–H2 linker region also result from hydrophobic residue interactions, and these are enhanced in the LacYPop system due to the antiparallel binding of the PopTags. Our MD simulations thus show that the hydrophobic character of the PopTag is important for its self-association properties.

The PopTag helices embed at the membrane surface due to their amphipathic nature, creating membrane-mediated PopTag–PopTag interactions (Fig. 2a). This membrane interaction potentially competes with the solution-mediated condensate formation, as hydrophobic residues engaged with the membrane are unavailable for PopTag–PopTag interactions. It is feasible that a dynamic equilibrium exists between membrane-mediated and solution-mediated condensate formation. To explore this, we performed additional simulations of LacYPop where proteins were configured at high concentration with the PopTags extended into the solvent (Supplementary Fig. 6). This indeed reduced membrane association and allowed more extensive PopTag–PopTag interactions and network formation through association of the helical parts. We thus propose a two-step process for the condensate formation of LacYPop: Initially, PopTags interact with the membrane while exploring protein–protein contacts (Fig. 2a). As the local concentration increases, protein–protein interactions dominate over membrane association, leading to PopTags interacting in solution (Supplementary Fig. 6).

Together, our simulations demonstrate that the PopTags mediate interactions between otherwise non-associating LacY proteins through their hydrophobic interfaces. This creates a dynamic network of protein–protein interactions that drives the condensate-like behavior of LacYPop membrane proteins.

Membrane curvature impacts the distribution of LacY condensates
What determines the predominant polar localization of phase-separated LacY-mEos3.2-PopTag? We tested whether the nucleoid would exclude the condensates from the lateral membrane. We imaged BW25113 LacYmEos and BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop cells after treatment with cephalexin for 4 and 7 h (Fig. 3a, b). Cephalexin leads to elongation of E. coli and accumulation of multiple nucleoids in one cell24. After 4 h of cephalexin treatment, we observed cells with two nucleoids per cell, using DAPI as a DNA-staining dye. LacYmEos is homogeneously distributed in the membrane, while LacYmEos-Pop has the same distribution as in untreated cells: the majority of the condensates are at the cell poles, but some smaller foci are found at the lateral membrane. After 7 h of cephalexin treatment, the number of nucleoids per cell increased, but for both LacY variants, the localization patterns remained, with the majority of LacYmEos-Pop at the poles and LacYmEos homogenously distributed. Importantly, we do not observe accumulation of LacYmEos-Pop in the inter-nucleoid regions, suggesting that LacYmEos-Pop localization is not governed by nucleoid exclusion.

To further investigate the role of the nucleoid in LacYmEos-Pop positioning, we visualized LacYmEos-Pop in nucleoid-free E. coli LY177 cells, where arabinose-induced expression of I-SceI endonuclease leads to nucleoid degradation25, which was confirmed by DAPI staining (Fig. 3c). Upon nucleoid degradation, LacYmEos-Pop is mostly in the polar regions with some foci on the lateral membrane, while LacYmEos remains homogenously distributed over the membrane. These experiments rule out that nucleoid exclusion causes polar location of the LacYmEos-Pop membrane condensates.

Next, we evaluated the effect of membrane curvature on the localization of the proteins, using spheroplasts (spherical, osmotically sensitive cells made by removing part of the outer membrane and peptidoglycan layer) prepared from BW25113 LacYmEos and BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop cells (Fig. 3d)26,27. Spheroplasts made from BW25113 LacYmEos served as a control and showed a homogenous LacYmEos distribution. Spheroplasts from BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop show a variety of LacY-mEos3.2-PopTag distributions, ranging from multiple clusters per spheroplast to almost homogeneous protein distribution. We then measured the same cells 30 min after spheroplast formation and found a dissolution of LacYmEos-Pop condensates from the original poles, and the cell shape change is associated with a more homogenous localization pattern.

To capture the redistribution of LacYmEos-Pop upon spheroplast formation over time, we immobilized E. coli cells with agarose pads, supplemented with the “cocktail” for spheroplast formation to trigger the shape change. The time-lapse videos clearly show the gradual redistribution of large phase-separated condensates from distinct foci to homogeneously localized protein over ~40 min (Supplementary Video 2). Thus, the loss of pole localization of phase-separated membrane-bound condensates coincides with the loss of the pole curvature. To reintroduce curvature in spheroplasts with homogeneously distributed LacYmEos-Pop, we induced plasmolysis of the spheroplasts immobilized under agarose pads supplemented with 0.5 M NaCl. The LacYmEos-Pop distribution was monitored by wide-field fluorescence microscopy (Fig. 3e). Remarkably, upon plasmolysis, LacYmEos-Pop condensates are no longer homogeneously distributed in the spheroplasts but predominantly localize at highly curved, concave membrane regions (Supplementary Fig. 7). Spearman correlation coefficient between the normalized curvature and normalized fluorescence intensity along the deformed spheroplasts contour is 0.24, p-value < 0.0001. These observations highlight the importance of membrane curvature in the spatial distribution of LacYmEos-Pop.

Activity of condensed LacY
To evaluate the effect of condensation on LacY transport activity, we used 14C-lactose and determined the uptake of the substrate by LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop in E. coli BW25113 ΔlacY (Fig. 4a). The cells producing LacYmEos-Pop import slightly more lactose compared to the cells with LacYmEos, which is seen as higher plateauing levels of the uptake curves (UMAX = 2.96±0.17 versus 2.48±0.10 nmol lactose/mg total cell protein, extra sum-of-squares F-test p-value=0.0145, Fig. 4b). The expression levels of the LacY variants are similar as determined by fluorescence analysis of cell lysates, for which the proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE. We measured 3.5±0.4×103 LacYmEos and 3.4±0.5×103 LacYmEos-Pop proteins per E. coli cell (Supplementary Fig. 8). Quantification of LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop by in-gel fluorescence shows that they do not greatly exceed the native-level expression, which is ~2500 LacY molecules per cell in the fully induced state28.

Further, we tested whether LacY condensation can rescue the decrease of activity under stress conditions, i.e. hyperosmotic stress29. We measured 14C-lactose uptake of cells without stress and upon an increase of NaCl concentration of 160 or 320 mM, resulting in a 2- or 3-fold increase in osmolarity (Fig. 4c). Under the higher osmolarity, the maximum levels of lactose uptake UMAX reduce both for BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos and BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos-Pop cells (Fig. 4d). Remarkably, under all measured conditions, LacYmEos-Pop outperforms LacYmEos. We then visualized the protein distribution in osmotically stressed BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos and BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos-Pop cells (Fig. 4e). Both strains show some membrane deformations indicative of plasmolysis, and the effects are more pronounced with the 3-fold than with the 2-fold osmolarity increase. However, we find fewer deformed BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos-Pop cells than BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos; 24±7% versus 53±8% at the 3-fold osmolarity increase (number of analyzed fields of view is 5, two-sided t-test p-value=0.0003). We find almost no deformed BW25113 ΔlacY LacYmEos-Pop cells at a two-fold osmolarity increase, which suggests that membrane-bound biomolecular condensates support the cytoplasmic membrane and reduce its deformation under hyperosmotic stress. A smaller degree of plasmolysis will diminish the volume decrease, and this may explain the higher UMAX of LacYmEos-Pop-expressing cells.

PopTag is driving the co-condensation of LacY and LacZ in vivo
Heterocondensation of cytoplasmic and membrane proteins has to the best of our knowledge not been explored but could potentially speed up reaction networks by direct pass on of substrates from transporter to enzyme. Hence, we co-expressed LacY and LacZ fusions with mEos3.2 and mRuby fluorescent proteins, respectively, with and without C-terminal PopTag (Table 1). We visualized the localization of membrane (LacY) and cytoplasmic (LacZ) protein for all combinations with and without PopTag by confocal laser-scanning fluorescence microscopy (Fig. 5a). LacYmEos distributed homogeneously across the membrane, and LacYmEos-Pop was predominantly present at the cell poles with smaller clusters in the lateral membrane, independent of co-expression of either LacZmRuby or LacZmRuby-Pop. LacZmRuby is distributed mostly homogeneously in the cytoplasm, independent of co-expression of LacYmEos or LacYmEos-Pop; some inclusion bodies are visible at the cell poles, which is expected as β-galactosidase fusions are prone to aggregation30,31, even at low inducer concentration (0.000001% w/v L-rhamnose) and 30 °C in minimal media. Remarkably, LacZmRuby-Pop is localized differently in cells producing LacYmEos and LacYmEos-Pop. In BW25113 LacYmEos-LacZmRuby-Pop cells, LacZmRuby-Pop forms spherical condensates at the cell poles, while in BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop-LacZmRuby-Pop cells we observe two different morphologies (Fig. 5a). In the first, more frequent scenario, LacZmRuby-Pop forms large dome-shaped condensates at the cell poles and smaller condensates in the lateral membrane colocalizing with LacYmEos-Pop. In the second, less frequent, scenario, LacZmRuby-Pop forms spherical condensates at the cell poles without smaller condensates in the lateral membrane. We hypothesize that in scenario I LacZmRuby-Pop fully covers the in-membrane condensate of LacYmEos-Pop, and in scenario II, large cytosolic condensates of LacZmRuby-Pop only partially interact with in-membrane condensates of LacYmEos-Pop. Co-localization of LacY and LacZ in all measured conditions was quantified by Pearson correlation coefficient with Costes thresholding. A high positive correlation was observed for LacYmEos-Pop-LacZmRuby-Pop (r=0.81) and no or negative correlation for other conditions: −0.12 for LacYmEos-LacZmRuby, −0.02 for LacYmEos-LacZmRuby-Pop, and −0.41 for LacYmEos-Pop-LacZmRuby.

FRAP measurements of the polar LacYmEos-Pop condensates, co-expressed with LacZmRuby-Pop, showed similar recovery patterns as observed with LacYmEos-Pop alone (Supplementary Fig. 9). The half-time of recovery was 134±47 s for LacYmEos-Pop alone and 103±19 s for LacYmEos-Pop in heterocondensates (the extra sum-of-squares F-test p-value=0.71), and the extents of recovery were 0.1409±0.009 for LacYmEos-Pop alone and 0.128±0.009 for LacYmEos-Pop in heterocondensates (extra sum-of-squares F-test p-value=0.35). These data indicate that LacYmEos-Pop condensates have similar material properties when expressed alone or with LacZmRuby-Pop.

Transmission electron microscopy of BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop-LacZmRuby-Pop also shows two scenarios of heterocondensate formation (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. 10). Scenario I was observed in 5 out of 15 cell sections and shows the electron-dense region at the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane, and it is thicker (~50 nm) than that of BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop cells (~10 nm, Fig. 5b, left). Interestingly, in one cell, a large electron-dense region is seen in the cytoplasm, which is partially in contact with a thin (~10 nm) electron-dense region on the inner membrane (Fig. 5b, right); this may represent scenario II of the confocal images (Fig. 5a). These two scenarios correlate with two types of LacZmRuby-Pop condensates, dome-shaped (more frequent) and spherical (less frequent) that are observed by confocal laser-scanning microscopy at the cell poles of BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop-LacZmRuby-Pop cells (Fig. 5a). The two scenarios can be rationalized when LacY and LacZ have different expression levels: Scenario I would occur when the levels are similar, and Scenario II if LacZ is expressed at a higher level than LacY. We conclude that LacYPop and LacZPop form heterocondensates of varying architectures that are anchored to the inner membrane of E. coli.

We then assessed the activity of LacY and LacZ in the heterocondensates. We constructed E. coli strains without mEos3.2 and mRuby to enable fluorescent read-out of LacZ activity with 4-methylumbelliferyl β-D-galactopyranoside as substrate32,33. The strains are named BW25113 ΔlacY LacY-LacZ, BW25113 ΔlacY LacYPop-LacZ, BW25113 ΔlacY LacY-LacZPop and BW25113 ΔlacY LacYPop-LacZPop (for details see Table 1). LacY activity was similar across all these strains as evaluated by 14C-lactose uptake measurements (Supplementary Fig. 11). The fluorescent substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl β-D-galactopyranoside (β-MUG), is transported by LacY33 and hydrolyzed by LacZ. The transport negative strain, BW25113 ΔlacY, shows a slight decrease in signal over time, which does not reflect β-galactosidase activity. Strains expressing LacY and LacZ, with or without PopTag, hydrolyze β-MUG, and we estimated the β-galactosidase activity from the slope of the linear increase of fluorescent signal over time (Supplementary Fig. 12). The fluorescence data were adjusted for the amounts of expressed β-galactosidase, determined by fluorescence imaging of SDS–PAGE separated E. coli lysates of LacZ-mRuby fusions, to obtain the specific β-galactosidase activity (Supplementary Fig. 13). The activities of LacZ in all strains were normalized to the mean activity in BW25113 ΔlacY LacY-LacZ cells, which was 1.00±0.03 a.u. The activity increases to 1.62±0.05 a.u. in BW25113 ΔlacY LacY-LacZPop cells, but decreases to 0.80±0.02 and 0.82±0.04 a.u. in BW25113 ΔlacY LacYPop-LacZ and BW25113 ΔlacY LacYPop-LacZPop cells, respectively (Fig. 5c). Clearly, the activity of β-galactosidase is highest when the protein is present in homocondensate and somewhat reduced in heterocondensates with LacY.
