Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors probe the impact of condensation at cellular membrane on the activity of the protein LacY in
E. Coli. LacY is a transmembrane protein. To achieve this, they fuse a pop tag (the c-terminal domain of
popZ) to LacY and probe the condensation of the protein. using a combination of experimental and
computational methods. They also probe the effect of co-condensation (ie of a membrane, LacY, and
cytosolic protein, LacZ) on protein activity. For this they make fusions of LacY and LacZ, with and without
pop tags and express them together in various combinations. The main highlights of the paper are:
I. The LacY-pop fusion forms condensates with different propensities at the poles vs lateral regions of the
membrane
II. They provide evidence suggesting that this is due to differences in membrane curvature in these two
regions
III. They also show that the LacY-pop fusion leads to slightly higher substrate transport, compared to the
LacY without the pop tag
IV. The LacY-pop fusion also leads to better lactose uptake under osmotic stress conditions
V. They observe co-condensation of LacY and LacZ, but this co-condensation does not lead to increased
activity; it even seems to suppress the activity.
In general, the manuscript is well written, and it is an interesting study. However, some of the conclusions
are not fully supported by the data presented and certain methodological details are missing, as outlined
below:
Major remarks:
1. The authors measure the protein diffusion at the poles and in the lateral regions for LacY-pop and find
that they are similar. They should also perform FRAP separately for the poles and the lateral condensates.
This will add further confidence that the material properties are similar.
We find that the diffusion inside the condensates is the same at the poles and in the lateral membrane,
which is based on the single-molecule measurements (Figure 1f,g). Bleaching of individual condensates at
the lateral membrane is not possible, due to their small size. However, FRAP of the lateral membrane
showed no recovery (new Figure 1d and text in lines 135 - 141), which might be due to the very strong
partitioning of LacYPop in the polar condensates.
2. For the MD simulation the initial set up is not ideal for an unbiased comparison. They start with the
proteins evenly spaced, using the same spacing for the LacY and LacY-pop. However, the Lac-Y pop will on
average have a larger radius of gyration, which means that the probability that the proteins can find each
other and interact will naturally be greater. The authors should use a non-biased initial set up where the
spacing scales with the average protein size. Additionally, another robust test would be start from a case
where the proteins are already clustered and measure whether the clustering at equilibrium are
significantly different.
We thank the reviewer for this comment on a potential bias in our initial simulation setup. We have
extended our simulations to 50 μs, which is sufficiently long to observe multiple binding and unbinding
events of the membrane proteins, ensuring the initial configuration does not bias our analysis of cluster
stability and size. The new data presented in Figure 2
3. The criteria used for determining if a cluster is formed in the MD simulation seems quite weak. They
put two proteins in cluster if at least they share one residue-residue contact. What is the average strength
of such a contact in comparison to the average thermal energy (KT)? Ideally, such interactions should be
multiples of KT to constitute a viable contact.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Our clustering criterion was designed to capture
large-scale differences in clustering behavior between LacY and LacYPop in an interpretable manner. This
approach revealed the clustering differences, which were validated with extended 50 μs simulations
during revision.
The energetic basis for these clustering differences is significant. Our contact map analysis (Figure 2c)
shows that PopTag-PopTag interactions occur primarily through the amphipathic α-helices, mainly the
hydrophobic interfaces of helix 1 and 2. Each helix contains approximately 15 residues. Literature values
for hydrophobic interactions range from 0.5-2 kT per residue
(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2011.02.053), meaning a single helical interface has a significant favorable
energy. Additionally, the proteins in larger clusters engage through multiple PopTag-PopTag contacts
simultaneously.
4. Related to that are the number of protein-protein interactions normalized by protein size? For instance,
the mutant with the pop tag will naturally have more contacts because it has more residues. Please discuss
in greater detail whether the reported protein-protein contacts are normalized or not.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this clarification. The reported protein-protein contacts are not
normalized by protein size as they are counted per membrane protein, not per residue. Our primary focus
was on the qualitative clustering behavior, whether proteins form contacts or not, rather than quantifying
absolute residue contact numbers. We have clarified this point in the revised text (legend to the Figure
2d).
5. Based on figure 2 and the SI, the authors claim that pop-tag interactions are primarily driven by helix 1.
The data presented only partially supports this. Based on fig 2c, a large fraction of the contacts are
localized in the region between H1 and H2. They do not comment on this. They also report that the
interactions are primarily hydrophobic in nature. However, the intermediate regions, seem to be charged
regions. Are they? Or at least regions with low hydrophobicity. If so, it seems that charged or other
interactions are a key.
We thank the reviewer for this observation. The extended simulations performed during revision now
reveal much more pronounced helix 2 involvement in LacYPop, with clear helix 1-helix 2 and helix 2-helix 2
interactions. The H1-H2 linker also shows contacts due to its hydrophobic residues, alongside charged
residues (ASP36, LYS35, ARG38). Additionally, when helices 1 and 2 from different PopTag domains
interact antiparallel, their connecting linker regions are brought into proximity, increasing the contacts.
We conclude that hydrophobic interactions are the primary driving force for PopTag condensation. We
have clarified this in the revised text to acknowledge the contributions of the H1-H2 linker region to the
contact map. See changes in lines 184 – 185 and 190 – 192.
6. In Fig 2b, it is unclear why the slab geometry was used to determine the contacts for the pop-tag
condensate in figure 2c. Ideally, this measurement is done on an isotropic system to avoid the effects of
having interfaces.
We used a slab geometry as a standard protocol for building condensates without knowing the
equilibrium density beforehand, while maximizing the internal condensate region and minimizing
interface effects. To validate this approach, we calculated the condensate density from the slab
simulations and constructed an isotropic condensate simulation at this density. This simulation was run
for 20 μs and used to calculate a reference contact map. Comparison of the contact maps shows that
interaction patterns qualitatively agree between both geometries, confirming that our slab-derived
contact analysis accurately represents the inter-PopTag interactions.
7. In the experiments, it would be useful to characterize the material properties of the heterogeneous
condensates, as done for the single-protein ones. This may help shed light on why the activity is affected
in the manner reported.
We now performed FRAP measurements in cells with LacYPop with co-expression of LacZPop. We observed
the same recovery pattern as for cell expressing LacYPop alone, that is, similar half-times of recovery (122
± 36 seconds for LacYmEos-Pop alone vs. 103 ± 19 seconds for LacYmEos-Pop in heterocondensate, extra sum-of-
squares F test p-value = 0.7620) and extents of recovery (0.132 ± 0.007 for LacYmEos-Pop alone vs. 0.128 ±
0.009 for LacYmEos-Pop in heterocondensate, extra sum-of-squares F test p-value = 0.6958) (lines 320 - 327
and Supplementary Figure S7). Information about the statistical test is added to the “Statistical analysis”
section lines 746-748 Thus, on the basis of FRAP experiments, we find no difference in the material
properties of LacYPop in homo- and heterocondensate.
8. The structures from alphafold3 used for setting up the simulations were these relaxed via all-atom
simulations before using martinize2? Are the secondary structures static in the martini simulations or are
they allowed to fluctuate?
The AlphaFold3 structures were used directly without prior all-atom relaxation. We validated these
structures by comparing them to available crystal structures of LacY, which showed good agreement with
the experimental models.
In our Martini simulations, secondary structures are constrained using an elastic network model,
preventing changes in secondary structure elements. However, the proteins are still allowed to fluctuate
and move within these constraints, maintaining realistic dynamics at the coarse-grained level. While
allowing changes in secondary structure could provide additional model accuracy, we deemed this beyond
the scope of the current study since our primary focus was on protein-protein interactions mediated by
PopTag domains. See changes in lines 652 – 659.
9. What is the rationale for the pressure set up used in the slab simulations? What are these so-called
default pressure parameters?
The slab simulation pressure setup makes the system incompressible in the xy-directions, keeping the
interface area fixed, while allowing the z-axis (box height) to equilibrate and establish the correct
condensate density. This prevents artificial expansion or contraction of the slab interface while enabling
the condensate to find its natural thickness. The "default pressure parameters" refer to standard Martini3
pressure coupling settings (1 bar, τ_p = 12 ps, β = 3×10⁻⁴ bar⁻¹) applied in the xy-plane, while pressure
coupling in the z-direction is disabled to preserve the slab geometry. This information is now added in
lines 686 - 689.
10. The authors state that the Martini-parameters were tuned using the idr-tune flag. Please discuss in
greater detail what this means. Tuned in what sense?
The idr-tune flag is an option in Martinize2 that optimizes Martini force field parameters specifically for
intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Standard Martini parameters tend to over compact IDRs compared
to experimental observations. The idr-tune flag addresses this by adjusting the bonded interactions in the
Martini3 protein model to better reproduce the expanded conformations of disordered regions. This
parameter optimization has been validated to improve the correspondence with all-atom simulations and
experimental data (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58199-2). This information is now added in lines
666-667.
Minor remarks:
1. The caption of Figure 2 needs further details so readers can immediately tell what they are looking at.
For instance, mentioning that proteins are embedded in a membrane etc.
We thank the reviewer for indicating that this was not clear, we improved the figure legend to clarify.
2. Describe what are spheroplasts at first usage.
Description of spheroplasts has been added in lines 235-236
3. Labels are needed throughout Figure 1. It is difficult to tell what exactly one should be looking for in Fig
1G for instance.
We added arrows pointing to the edges of the membrane-anchored LacYmEos-Pop condensates in right panel
of Figure 1h, and we refer to them in the legend.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Key results
In this study the authors examine phase separation of membrane proteins in live E. coli cells by expressing
fusions composed of membrane protein LacY and a PopTag scaffold domain to drive phase separation.
They examine the effect of this tag on the localization, dynamics, and activity of LacY, and explore the
activity of downstream enzyme LacZ with or without the same tag. The manuscript is clearly written and
the topic is of interest, particularly on how engineered co-condensation at a membrane might affect
enzyme activity in a cascade. However, the authors’ mechanistic arguments should be strengthened with
additional evidence, and additional quantification/clarification is needed. The following are some points
for revision.
Major points
1. The introduction should include a review of the existing literature on membrane-localized biomolecular
condensates (surface wetting, biological significance, curvature remodeling, etc.). I would disagree with
the characterization that membrane protein phase separation is uncharted territory given the examples
mentioned in the introduction. I also wonder whether a dynamic protein monolayer counts as a
condensate if it does not recruit components from the bulk, as the classification can become unclear at
the nanoscale (though this broad question does not need to be addressed in this manuscript).
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We expanded the introduction with membrane-localized
condensates (lines 67 - 77). “Uncharted territory” is perhaps too strong, but the amount of mechanistic
insight in membrane-localized condensates is minimal. Text has been changed in lines 52 - 53. We now
refer to the membrane condensates as 2D condensates, but we notice that (based on our analysis) they
display all the features of classical 3D condensates except that components are recruited from the
membrane and not from the cytoplasm.
2. In Figure 1G, arrows or other indicators would be helpful as the thin layer is hard to see. What methods
were used to classify whether the layer was present in each image and measure its thickness?
We added arrows to Figure 1h (previously Figure 1g) indicating the edges of the electron-dense regions
on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane.
To classify the EM images, we inspected them visually and, first, selected those with intact membrane
integrity and periplasmic space. Then, the layer was identified as a distinct electron-dense region on the
cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane. The analysis was blinded to the experiment group and
independently performed by two researchers, only cells labeled as condensate positive by both
researchers were marked as “positive” in the final analysis.
To estimate the thickness of the layer, we analyzed line profiles of the electron density perpendicular to
the membrane using ImageJ. All this information is now added in the Methods section (lines 642 – 647).
3. The MD simulations do not include mEos3.2, but this domain contributes significant size and surface
charge to the whole protein construct, and these features can affect phase separation/protein-protein
interactions. Can the authors discuss how the MD results might change if they included this domain?
We thank the reviewer for this comment. mEos3.2 serves purely as a fluorescent reporter and is not
expected to influence the PopTag-mediated clustering mechanism we are investigating. mEos3.2 was
designed as a true monomeric protein (10.1038/nmeth.2021). Omitting mEos3.2 from our simulations
reduced the computational complexity.
4. Residue-membrane interactions competing with scaffold protein condensate formation is an
interesting idea. Since the alternate simulation setup in Fig S4 resulted in quite different interaction
networks from those in Fig 2, can the authors comment on which interactions might correspond better to
the observations in vivo?
We suggest a two-step process for the condensate formation of LacYPop: Initially, PopTags interact with
the membrane while exploring protein-protein contacts (Fig 2). As the local concentration increases,
protein-protein interactions dominate over membrane association, leading to PopTags interacting in
solution (Fig S4). Sampling these different states in separate simulations is necessary due to MD timescale
limitations. The full process of LacY-bound PopTags detaching from the membrane and forming
condensates in solution is beyond current simulation timescales. In cells, we expect PopTags initially
sample both membrane and protein interactions, with condensate formation occurring when protein-
protein interactions outcompete membrane association. These points are better articulated in the revised
manuscript (lines 203 - 206).

condensate formation. Quantifying fluorescence intensity against local membrane curvature in the
datasets from Fig. 3d,e could support the claim that only the high-curvature regions promote condensate
formation (and provide an opportunity for larger sample size and a statistical test). Also, during osmotic
upshift there can be many changes to the intracellular chemical environment (ionic strength, pH,
crowding, etc.) which are known to govern biomolecular condensate phase separation. Are there ways to
confirm that the observed condensate formation is not due to one of these factors?
We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. We analyzed the correlation between local membrane
curvature and fluorescence intensity in LacYmEos-Pop spheroplasts, using the Kappa plugin for ImageJ

normalized curvature as a Supplementary Figure S5, and we present the data in lines 256 - 258.
We agree that effects of ionic strength, pH, crowding and other parameters are affected by osmotic
upshift, and we cannot rule out that they play a role in the formation of 2D membrane condensates.
We also do not see ways to dissect these parameters in in vivo studies. Importantly, we do find the formation
of the condensates at the cell poles in non-stressed cells, that is, at “normal” ionic strength, pH and
crowding levels. We feel that local curvature effects are the most plausible explanation. We now discuss
these points in more detail (lines 428 - 433).

Minor points

Scale bar sizes have been added to all the figure legends.

The percentages in Figure 1c were calculated from single-protein localization microscopy. This
